transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I spend so much time trying to fix how I look before I go out that I end up missing things with my family and at work. It's really starting to take a toll on my life, and I know I need to get some help for it.
When you are trying to fix how you look, is there a specific part of your appearance or a particular flaw that you feel is very noticeable or ugly, even if others tell you it looks fine?

Yes, I'm completely fixated on my face—I'm convinced my nose is crooked, my skin is saggy and blotchy, and my jaw is drooping. Even though people tell me I look fine for my age, all I see is this older, lopsided face. It just makes me feel incredibly self-conscious and out of place.
Is your avoidance of social situations entirely due to worries about how your face looks, or do you also fear being judged for your behavior, like saying the wrong thing?

No, it's not about my behavior or saying the wrong thing at all. My anxiety and the reason I cancel plans is entirely because I feel too unattractive and "off" to be seen in public. I just can't stand the thought of people looking at my crooked nose or sagging skin.

Aside from your concerns about your appearance, do you experience other repetitive thoughts or behaviors, such as an intense need to wash your hands, check locks, or arrange things in a specific order?
No, I don't have any of those urges like washing my hands or checking locks. My rituals are strictly focused on trying to fix or check how my face looks before I can leave the house.

The patient has confirmed that their repetitive behaviors and anxiety are exclusively focused on their perceived physical flaws (crooked nose, sagging skin, drooping jaw) and denied any general obsessive-compulsive symptoms (such as handwashing or checking locks) or social anxiety related to behavior. This rules out F42 (Obsessive-compulsive disorder) and confirms F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder, which includes Body Dysmorphic Disorder under ICD-10).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent preoccupation with perceived physical defects in their appearance (crooked nose, saggy skin, and drooping jaw) that are not noticeable to others. This preoccupation leads to repetitive behaviors (checking and trying to fix their face) and significant social avoidance, causing marked impairment in social and occupational functioning. These symptoms are characteristic of Body Dysmorphic Disorder, which is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder) in ICD-10.
